newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD - Australia markets to continue rate cut focus.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD - Australia markets to continue rate cut focus.

text.p: The timing of the next Australian interest rates reduction is likely to continue to preoccupy most market participants this week, although U.S. data will be a focus later in the week.

After the flurry of activity surrounding the release of inflation and wages data last week, markets are expected to be watching their screens each morning at 9.30 a.m. (2230 GMT) just in case the Reserve Bank decides to ease policy.

A 1996 interest rate cut remains firmly on the markets' agenda, with economists surveyed by Reuters seeing a 60 percent chance of a cut by the end of November, and a 75 percent chance of a cut by year end.
Datawise, Friday's retail trade is probably the major release of the week.
The current account deficit is expected to have remained well contained at around A$1.3 billion, and off the market's list of possible worries, economists said.
The trade balance should remain in surplus for the fourth successive months, unless exports fall by around three percent.

Retail trade is seen falling in September after rising strongly in the last two months. However that strength should see real retail trade rise by around 1.3 percent in the quarter, implying a sizeable contribution to third quarter GDp.
A strong monthly retail figure may dent some expectations of a cut, but economists said the market should remain bullish about the prospect of a rate cut ahead of next Tuesday's RBA board meeting.
The spotlight is also likely to be on the U.S. with third quarter GDP data due on Wednesday and non-farm payrolls data on Friday.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash yield 7.45 pct, 3-yr 6.73)

After last week's strong rally in Australian bonds the market could find itself in a period of consolidation as it waits for next week's Reserve Bank board meeting which is seen by many as endorsing a cut in official interest rates. While profit-taking and the possibility of a Treasury bond tender could put some upward pressure on yields, the prospect of easier monetary conditions after the board meets on November 5 should curb the extent of the retracement.

Yields dropped to their lowest level in 32 months last week as the market factored in a 50 basis point easing when both quarterly inflation and wages data proved contained well within the RBA comfort limits, and two key elements to suggest that the central bank may ease.
Next week's data is unlikely stir the market in this thinking.
The market could should start the week with an positive bias after U.S. Treasuries closed substantially higher after tame housing data and reports of central bank buying.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri US$0.7940, New York US$0.7900)
The Australian dollar faces another week of tension as the market continues its angonising wait for the Reserve Bank's decision on interest rates.
Speculation of a cut has kept the currency shackled in a US$0.7850-$0.7985 range for the last six weeks and, perversely, is unlikely to escape unless the easing becomes reality.

Dealers expected a knee-jerk selloff to around US$0.7880 on a 0.5 point cut, but most thought support at the September low of US$0.7850 would hold intact given that the currency would still offer a sizeable yield premium to offshore investors.
Indeed, some felt the dollar could rally once the uncertainty over policy was out the way, although that upbeat view was dependent on the assumption any easing would be the last in the cycle.
Resistance was lined up at US$0.7985, last week's peak, and US$0.7990 with the crucial bull targets being US$0.8020 and the May high of US$0.8050.

The currency also looked well-placed against the yen as Japanese interest rates were expected to remain at record lows for months to come and investors there were keen on higher yielding offshore assets such as A$ bonds.
It faced stiff psychological resistance at 90.00 yen, a four year old barrier, but dealers through a break eminently possible given the U.S. dollar had cleared its major barrier at 113.00 yen.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ordinaries 2335.2, down 42.4 on the day, and down 19.8 points on the week)
It's all eyes on Wall Street for local players this week with plenty of concern over whether the Dow will continue to lose ground as it did for most of last week.

Friday saw U.S. blue chips snap their four-session losing streak, the Dow closing above the phycollogically significant 6000 level following an unexpectedly strong quarterly earnings report from Dow component Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing.
U.S. market analysts warned that Wall Street was still seen in a short-term corrective cycle and was vulnerable on the downside to any signs of inflation.
"The market is looking very much to Wall Street," said dealer Paul Ford of Shaw Stockbroking, adding that any real trend was difficult to discern.
"I think at the moment the market is very much a day to day proposition."

Behind the 42 point drop for the All Ordinaries index was the failure of the Reserve Bank to deliver another interest rate cut following weak inflation and wages data earlier last week.

Major economic data due this week is the current account data for September on Wednesday and retail trade on Friday although both are seen as having only a very muted impact on the market's interest rate expectations.
The annual meeting season continues in full swing, those of note include:
Tuesday-Goldfields Ltd, QBE Insurance, QCT Resources Ltd, and Tabcorp Holdings
Wednesday-RGC Ltd
Thursday-Fletcher Challenge, Lend Lease, National Foods, North Ltd
Friday-Leighton Holdings, Sons of Gwalia.
